targetQuery: unit vs integration vs end-to-end tests / testing pyramid vs testing trophy / integration test against a real database
comparedAgainst: https://martinfowler.com/bliki/TestPyramid.html — Fowler's own page, fetched and checked verbatim: the Cohn-in-conversation-with-Lisa-Crispin-2003-4 origin story, the Jason-Huggins-independently-around-2006 line, and the 'broad-stack tests are expensive, slow, and brittle... there are exceptions' assumption all match the article's paraphrase exactly. Fowler's page is a short bliki entry with no runnable code and no real database; this article goes well beyond it with a working xUnit v3 + SQLite integration suite, a fake-vs-real fidelity demonstration and two genuine flakiness demos.

https://kentcdodds.com/blog/write-tests — Dodds' actual post, fetched directly. The trophy's four-band structure (static, unit, integration, E2E), the confidence-quotient/bang-for-your-buck framing, 'Integration tests strike a great balance on the trade-offs between confidence and speed/expense,' the fact that Dodds does not dispute E2E should stay rare, and the fact that the trophy publishes no competing percentage split are all accurately represented — this part of the writer's stated intent holds up. But the specific sentence attributed to Dodds in quotation marks ('It doesn't matter if your component `<A />` renders component `<B />` with props if `<B />` breaks without prop `e`.') is not what the post says; see issues.

https://testing.googleblog.com/2015/04/just-say-no-to-more-end-to-end-tests.html — fetched the raw HTML directly (not just the rendered summary) to confirm the '70/20/10 split: 70% unit tests, 20% integration tests, and 10% end-to-end tests. The exact mix will be different for each team, but in general, it should retain that pyramid shape' sentence is in Mike Wacker's own post body, not a reader comment — a check worth doing explicitly since an automated fetch of this page initially (and incorrectly) suggested the line was comment-only. The article's citation is accurate.

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/testing/choosing-a-testing-strategy — fetched in full. The 'SQLite as a database fake' heading, the 'testing against SQLite does not guarantee the same results as against SQL Server, or any other database' sentence, and the case-sensitivity example are all quoted accurately and in the place the article uses them.

Real-world comparison: most public treatments of the pyramid/trophy debate (including the two above) argue in the abstract or show toy examples. This article's fidelity-gap block (RealLinkRepository vs. a Dictionary-backed FakeLinkRepository, both driven through the same interface, printing 'rejects' vs. 'ACCEPTS') is a genuinely differentiated, actually-executed demonstration of the claim rather than an assertion of it — stronger than either compared source on this specific point.
justification: `node tools/run-code.mjs src/content/articles/testing/testing-pyramid-and-integration-tests.md` was run 7 times from PowerShell (not just the claimed 5), all 7 identical: `PASS testing/testing-pyramid-and-integration-tests.md  blocks=12 executed=6`. Read tools/run-code.mjs itself to confirm what that guarantees: the order-dependence block's `text output` has no `[...]` wildcards, so 'PASS CreatesALink / FAIL RejectsAnUnknownCode' then 'PASS / PASS' had to match byte-for-byte on every one of the 7 runs — genuine, reproducible non-flakiness, which is the right kind of rigor for an article about flaky tests. The timing-variance block correctly wildcards every measured number, so it can never itself be flaky under the harness; that is appropriate, not a dodge, since the surrounding prose only claims variance exists, not specific figures. I traced both the LinkRepository/SQLite schema and the fidelity-gap program by hand: `Create_DuplicateCode_ThrowsFromTheUniqueConstraint` genuinely requires the real `Code TEXT PRIMARY KEY` constraint — LinkRepository.Create contains no duplicate-checking code at all, so the Fact only passes because SQLite's own unique index rejects the second INSERT; a naive Dictionary-backed fake using `links[code] = targetUrl` (an indexer assignment, which overwrites in .NET rather than throwing, unlike `Dictionary.Add`) would silently accept the duplicate, exactly as the fidelity-gap program demonstrates and exactly as its own run-code output ('rejects ... real SQLite' / 'ACCEPTS ... hand-rolled fake') confirms was actually executed, not asserted. I fetched Fowler's 'Eradicating Non-Determinism in Tests' and confirmed all four quotes used (shared database state, the system clock, 'never use bare sleeps... use a callback or polling', resource leaks) verbatim. I fetched xUnit's 'Running Tests in Parallel' page and confirmed both quotes used (collections don't run in parallel against each other; one collection per class by default, so different classes can run in parallel) verbatim, and confirmed the article's IClassFixture/shared-static-connection reasoning exercise is a sound application of that documented behavior, not a stretch. I fetched Microsoft's 'Testing in .NET' and ASP.NET Core integration-tests pages and confirmed both boundary-defining quotes verbatim. I fetched sqlite.org's in-memory-database page and datatype3.html and confirmed the `:memory:`-isolation quotes and the BINARY-collation/memcmp() claim verbatim. All 13 front-matter sources are real, live pages. However, one factual error survives this pass: the sentence attributed to Dodds in quotation marks, 'It doesn't matter if your component `<A />` renders component `<B />` with props if `<B />` breaks without prop `e`,' is not what kentcdodds.com/blog/write-tests actually says. The real sentence is 'It doesn't matter if your component `<A />` renders component `<B />` with props `c` and `d` if component `<B />` actually breaks if prop `e` is not supplied' — the article drops the concrete `c` and `d` prop names and rewords 'actually breaks if prop `e` is not supplied' to 'breaks without prop `e`,' inside quotation marks that assert this is Dodds' own wording. Per the editorial brief's hard rule against fabricated quotes, this caps the score at 7 regardless of the rest of the piece's real strengths. Two smaller sourcing issues stack on top of that: the front-matter sources 'Overview - Microsoft.Data.Sqlite' and 'Getting Started with xUnit.net v3' are both listed but never cited inline anywhere in the body (confirmed by grepping the article for their titles and URLs — each appears exactly once, in the front matter), which the editorial brief's binding lessons call a finding in its own right. And the line 'Chapter 11 of [Mocks, Stubs and Fakes](/testing/test-doubles/) makes the general point...' misattributes a book chapter number to a web article: 'Chapter 11' belongs to Meszaros's *xUnit Test Patterns* (cited by that number inside the sibling test-doubles.md article itself, which is a web page with no chapters of its own), not to the linked page, so as written it reads as though the sibling article is organized into numbered chapters. None of this touches the article's real strengths, which are substantial: the testing-trophy critique is represented with real nuance (accurately stating Dodds does not dispute rare E2E and that the trophy publishes no competing ratio, which is the harder and more accurate reading of the source), the pyramid's origin chain (Cohn, crediting a 2003-4 conversation with Lisa Crispin per Fowler, plus Huggins' independent 2006 idea) is sourced and accurate, the SQLite-as-fake caveat matches EF Core's own docs precisely including the case-sensitivity example (independently re-derived and confirmed correct via the case-sensitivity code block), and the fake-vs-real fidelity demonstration is a genuinely executed, differentiated proof rather than the abstract assertion most competing treatments settle for. A strong round-1 draft with one real factual error keeping it off a higher score.

issues.location: "What do critics say is wrong with it?" section, the sentence: "It doesn't matter if your component `<A />` renders component `<B />` with props if `<B />` breaks without prop `e`."
issues.problem: This is presented in quotation marks as Kent C. Dodds' own wording, but it is not what kentcdodds.com/blog/write-tests says. The actual sentence, fetched and confirmed verbatim, is: "It doesn't matter if your component `<A />` renders component `<B />` with props `c` and `d` if component `<B />` actually breaks if prop `e` is not supplied." The article drops the concrete `c` and `d` prop names and rewords the second clause, while keeping the quotation marks — a fabricated quote per the editorial brief's hard rule 1 ("Nothing fabricated... quotes"), which caps the technical score at 7.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either quote the sentence exactly as Dodds wrote it (with `c` and `d`, and "actually breaks if prop `e` is not supplied"), or drop the quotation marks and paraphrase in the article's own words without implying it is Dodds' verbatim wording.

issues.problem: Both are listed as sources but neither title nor URL appears anywhere else in the article — grepped the full text and each string occurs exactly once, in the front matter. Per the editorial brief's binding lessons: 'A source in the list that is never cited inline... is a finding.'

issues.location: "Why not just mock the repository instead?" section: "Chapter 11 of [Mocks, Stubs and Fakes](/testing/test-doubles/) makes the general point this test relies on..."
issues.problem: This attaches a book chapter number to a link that points at this site's own sibling web article, which has no chapters. 'Chapter 11' actually names a chapter of Gerard Meszaros's *xUnit Test Patterns*, which the sibling article itself cites by that number (test-doubles.md line 553: '(*xUnit Test Patterns*, chapter 11)') — the chapter belongs to the book, not to the linked page. As written, a reader following the link expecting a numbered chapter 11 on the site will not find one.
issues.fixLooksLike: Say what is actually true, e.g. "The [test-doubles article](/testing/test-doubles/) makes the general point this test relies on, citing Meszaros's *xUnit Test Patterns* (chapter 11): a double is only as good as..."
